H I G H L I G H T S                                        G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T

• Amine CO2 capture retrofit cost model
  developed for any industrial facility.
• Capture cost model validated against
  published costs for actual retrofit
  projects.
• Capture plants shared by multiple facil­
  ities reduces average capture costs.
• Shared CO2 transport dramatically re­
  duces required pipeline mileage and
  costs.
• Cost benefits of shared infrastructure are
  most significant for smaller facilities.

    The capture block is designed to maximize shop fabrication over field
fabrication to reduce construction time and cost, as suggested by [57].
We imposed a maximum column diameter of 15 m [54]. We additionally
constrained column height to a maximum of 20 m, the tallest observed
in reported studies [46,58]. To achieve a proper liquid and gas distri­
bution, the pressure drop across a single column is limited to a maximum
of 0.002 bar and the liquid level to flooding is maintained below 70%
[59]. If the flooding factor would exceed 70% at a diameter of 15 m, an
additional column is introduced. Several studies, e.g., [54,60], suggest
20 stages in each absorption column and 10 in each stripper column, and
we confirmed these values are appropriate for maximizing absorption
and desorption in our capture block designs.
    We chose to design columns with stainless steel packing, based on
[60,61], and calculated performance of the packing section using the
Aspen + rate-based model [60,62], which was validated using experi­
mental data [63]. The goal of our modelling of the column was to esti­
mate a purchased equipment cost (PEC), for which we require an
estimate of column volume. For relatively large columns operating near
atmospheric pressure, as in our designs, the PEC per unit volume ($/m3)
is dominated by cost of the packing [64]. Therefore, we chose to esti­
mate column PEC (in Section 3.3) based on the volume of our modeled
packing section. Given uncertainties, this may higher or lower than a
cost estimate based on more detailed engineering.
    The CO₂ compression block is modeled with six centrifugal stages to
bring the captured CO₂ to 86 barg, followed by a pump to boost pressure
to 110 barg [35]. Pressure ratio per stage and isentropic and mechanical
efficiencies of 2, 80%, and 90%, are assumed, respectively, based on
[65]. The CO₂ dehydration block, which is placed between the last
centrifugal compressor stage and the pump, reduces the water content
from 25,000 ppm to <300 ppm to meet guidelines [66] for CO₂ transport
in carbon steel pipes and injection into saline reservoirs for storage. We
adopt a triethylene glycol (TEG) dehydration system, as used in the Shell
Quest CCS project [35]. The equipment arrangement and specifications
follow those of Bahadori et al. [67], and the required amount of TEG is
based on modelling by Kemper et al. [68]. See equipment configuration
details in SI.4.
    The power-to-heat output ratio of the cogeneration block is set to
exactly match the parasitic energy needs of the capture facility. Power-
to-heat ratios (MWe/MWth) vary by cogeneration technology [69].
Considering that the power-to-heat ratios in our plant designs are
approximately 0.2, we utilize boiler/back-pressure steam turbines with
design inlet steam pressure of 130 barg and back-pressure of 18 barg.
CO₂ emissions from a cogeneration facility are a function of the fuel type
it uses [70] and whether or not flue gas CO₂ is captured. We assume
natural gas is the boiler fuel, but future boiler modifications could offer
compatibility with lower-carbon fuels [71]. In most of our plant designs,
we assume that the cogeneration flue gas CO₂ is not captured, but we
also design and evaluate one case where flue gas CO₂ is captured along
with the target stream CO₂. Equipment configurations and design
specifications for our cogeneration plant are as described by Jechura
[72] and listed in the SI.6.
